reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a Bitcoin trading-pool opportunity by presenting daily compounding and a projection that $500 could become more than $361,000 over 60 months. The speaker connects participation with placing funds in the pool and directs viewers to click a link, join his team, or join an associated Facebook group. Although the speaker warns that Bitcoin is volatile and earnings are not guaranteed, the described promotion and solicitation support the classification.

citations.quote: earning some great Bitcoin with mir mere trading international
You can risk losing some or all of your Bitcoin.
if you got $1,000 into the trading pool
Tomorrow, you're going to have $1,006.74 working for you.
The more money you got in the trading pool, the more you're going to make.

opening.argument: Judge, the large projection should be read as a conditional forecast, not a promise. The speaker explicitly warns that participants could lose some or all of their Bitcoin and says earnings are not guaranteed. He also makes the five-year calculation depend on the company continuing at its current rate. Those qualifications matter when deciding whether the video presents a certain outcome or discusses a possible one.

citations.quote: Bitcoin is very volatile. You can risk losing some or all of your Bitcoin.
This is not a guaranteed way of saying that you're going to earn Bitcoin
if this company continues to stay at where a set right now for the next 5 years

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening identifies a projection, pool participation and an invitation to join. Those establish promotion, but they do not make the projected balance an assured return. The speaker expressly calls the exercise mathematics and repeats that nothing is guaranteed. The cited example of a balance working the next day illustrates compounding under the assumed rate; it does not establish that the rate will persist.

citations.quote: nothing is guaranteed. Like I said, we're just doing the math.
Tomorrow, you're going to have $1,006.74 working for you. It's going to compound.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The warnings qualify the forecast, but they do not change what the speaker is promoting. He tells viewers that more money in the trading pool means more earnings, projects a large five-year balance, and then asks them to join his team. The concern is the solicitation built around pool returns, not whether he literally guarantees the projected amount.

citations.quote: The more money you got in the trading pool, the more you're going to make.
60 months, you made over $361,749.95.
just click the link below. Get on my team.

opening.argument: Judge, much of the video functions as a worked demonstration: the speaker walks through a trading report, explains how a day's percentage changes with the amount placed in the pool, and enters a starting amount and period into a growth calculator. That sequence supports reading the striking final figure as a calculator output used to teach compounding, not proof that anyone received it. His own description is that he is showing possibilities.

citations.quote: Let's look at the last 50 entries
this is how I teach people how to add up how much you will make daily
about our growth calculator and we're gonna base it off of Bitcoin
I just want to give you guys possibilities.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly notes the pool and the projected balance, but neither turns a worked example into evidence of a realized five-year return. The speaker frames the calculation as what someone would have made under a stated trading-result example, then uses a 60-month input. The report and calculator explain how he arrives at the figure; they do not establish that the future result occurred.

citations.quote: let's say you would have had your money in a trading pool today
We're going to say for 60 months.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The calculator output is a projection, but the demonstration is embedded in a pitch to participate. The speaker says a larger pool contribution produces more earnings and directs viewers to a link and his team. Showing the arithmetic does not make the pool-return solicitation merely educational.

citations.quote: The more money you got in the trading pool, the more you're going to make.
if you want to learn more about MIRG Trading International, just click the link below. Get on my team.

opening.argument: Judge, the closing invitation can be read as an ordinary introduction to a service through a team contact: viewers are told they can ask questions before joining. The speaker describes the pool and his own reported results, but the supplied material does not show a viewer transferring funds, receiving a guaranteed payout or surrendering credentials to him. A promotional link and an ambitious illustration warrant scrutiny; they do not, by themselves, establish those additional steps.

citations.quote: you can ask me anything because this is one of my group pages for my team
Let's look at the last 50 entries because I've only been with the company for since October 11th
Nothing is guaranteed.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening shows that he invites viewers into a pool-related opportunity; it does not show what happens after a viewer follows the link or asks to join the group. His stated invitation is also to ask questions and learn what participation takes. The quoted hypothetical pool balance explains the proposed arrangement, but no cited passage establishes a completed viewer deposit or payout.

citations.quote: if you want to learn more about MIRG Trading International, just click the link below.
I will show you guys exactly what it takes to be part of our pool
Tomorrow, you're going to have $1,006.74 working for you.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A completed viewer deposit is unnecessary to identify what this video promotes. The speaker explicitly asks viewers to get started and join his team, while describing money placed in a trading pool as earning and compounding. The absence of a filmed transfer does not erase the investment-pool mechanism presented to viewers.
